Leukocyte count is 15,100/mm³ (65% segmented neutrophils, 10% bands, 25% lymphocytes). Chest x-rays are shown. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.E: CT scan of the chest with pulmonary embolism protocol

correctExplanation: Pneumonia classically presents with acute onset cough (generally productive of sputum), shortness of breath, chest discomfort, fever, chills, and fatigue. Vital signs may show fever, tachycardia, tachypnea, hypoxemia, and hypotension (if severe). On examination, rhonchi and rales may be detected in consolidated lung, along with egophony and dullness to percussion. Patients may have increased work of breathing or respiratory distress. The diagnosis is supported radiographically with airspace disease or consolidation visualized on x-ray, as shown here, or on CT. Pneumonia arises because of the presence of bacteria, virus, parasite, or fungi within pulmonary parenchyma, triggering an inflammatory reaction with resultant exudate into airspace. It is common in hospitalized patients because of risk factors for introduction of a pathogen, aspiration, and immunocompromise, including recent surgery, swallowing dysfunction, and intubation. Additionally, resistant pathogens often colonize hospitals and equipment, increasing the risk for refractory infection despite coadministration of antibiotics. Treatment of hospital-acquired pneumonia generally begins with the administration of broad-spectrum antibiotics (especially those covering methicillin resistant S. aureus [MRSA] and P. aeruginosa) while awaiting culture and sensitivity data from sputum samples if obtained. Suitable antibiotics for this purpose include vancomycin and third- or fourth-generation cephalosporins such as ceftazidime or cefepime. Antibiotics should then be narrowed to those that suitably target the infecting agent once a clinical response is achieved. Reduction in risk factors should occur, such as upright positioning of patients, removal of any unnecessary pharyngeal lines or tubes (eg, nasogastric tubes), and frequent respiratory therapy/pulmonary toileting. Postoperative pain, often worse when breathing, should be aggressively managed to permit full chest excursion, promote coughing and respiratory clearance, and limit atelectasis.

questionStem: A 67-year-old man comes to the physician because of nonproductive cough, hemoptysis, and a 9-kg (20-lb) weight loss over the past month. He has smoked two packs of cigarettes daily for 50 years. Breath sounds are decreased over the right posterior hemithorax. Laboratory studies show no abnormalities. An x-ray of the chest shows collapse of the right lower lobe of the lung. Which of the following is the most likely pathophysiology of this patient’s condition?
correctExplanation: Lung cancer often remains asymptomatic until advanced stage, at which time the tumor has locally invaded or metastasized, leading to the development of symptoms. The initial presentation is often nonspecific, including weight loss and fatigue. Once the tumor has invaded or involved neurosensory and vascular structures, patients may begin to experience coughing and hemoptysis. If the lesion is large enough to invade or obstruct a bronchus, patients may also experience post-obstructive or recurrent pneumonia in parenchyma distal to the lesion, caused by atelectasis and impaired endobronchial clearance of mucus, secretions, and inhaled pathogens. In this patient, the decreased breath sounds over the right posterior hemithorax suggest the presence of an endobronchial obstruction to airflow; this is further supported by atelectasis on x-ray in the corresponding area. Squamous cell carcinoma and small cell carcinoma of the lung tend to be centrally occurring lesions, often seen in smokers. Non-small cell carcinoma and other subtypes are more often peripherally occurring and may be more common in nonsmokers. Because of the significant morbidity and mortality with late diagnosis, screening low-dose chest CT is recommended by the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force in patients aged 50 to 80 years with a 20 pack-year smoking history and who currently smoke or have quit within the past 15 years.
incorrectExplanation:
Increased pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (Choice B) describes the pathophysiology of cardiogenic pulmonary edema: fluid accumulating in the interstitial and alveolar spaces of the lung because of increased left-heart pressures. On examination, rales may be heard, generally in dependent areas. X-ray generally discloses bilateral airspace edema, cephalization of the vessels, Kerley B lines, pleural effusions, and cardiomegaly.

Pleural inflammation with fluid formation (Choice C) describes the pathophysiology of pleurisy, mesothelioma, empyema, or similar extra-pulmonary pathology. While lung sounds may be decreased, the presence of fluid in the pleural space would be seen on x-ray.

Proximal airway inflammation (Choice D) describes the pathophysiology of bronchitis, which is characterized by cough and sputum production. Breath sounds are generally normal.

Pulmonary parenchymal necrosis (Choice E) describes the pathophysiology of cavitary lesions, such as those seen in tuberculosis or fungal infections. X-ray would show cavitary lesions.

Pulmonary vascular obstruction (Choice F) describes the pathophysiology of pulmonary embolism, which is characterized by sudden-onset dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, and hypoxemia. X-ray is often normal.

questionStem: A previously healthy 32-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 6-month history of shortness of breath and dry cough with exercise. He has smoked one pack of cigarettes weekly for 5 years. Vital signs are within normal limits. Faint bilateral expiratory wheezes are heard. Pulmonary function tests show a decreased FEV1, a normal FVC, and a decreased FEV1:FVC ratio (45% of predicted). The flow volume loop is shown. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Asthma, a reversible obstructive lung disease, presents with shortness of breath, cough, tachypnea, and hypoxemia (in severe cases), increased work of breathing, and wheezing on auscultation. Faint bilateral expiratory wheezes are heard in this patient, and the pulmonary function tests show a decreased FEV1, a normal FVC, and a decreased FEV1:FVC ratio, which is consistent with an obstructive pattern. The flow volume loop also supports this diagnosis.

questionStem: A 25-year-old man comes to the physician due to 2 months of shortness of breath and cough. He has no history of smoking. Physical examination shows bilateral wheezing. Pulmonary function tests are obtained and the flow-volume loop is shown below. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Asthma, a reversible obstructive lung disease, presents with shortness of breath, cough, tachypnea, and hypoxemia (in severe cases), increased work of breathing, and wheezing on examination. It is often triggered by exercise, allergens, illness, and smoke. It is characterized by a reversible bronchospasm which causes obstruction of airflow. Generally, exhalation is affected more than inhalation. The diagnosis is suspected based on clinical history and examination, and it is confirmed through pulmonary function tests (PFTs) which disclose an obstructive pattern characterized by a decrease in FEV1, decreased FEV1:FVC ratio, and preservation of FVC. Flow volume loops generally disclose abrupt decreases in the expiratory flow rate compared to those of an unaffected patient, which creates a concave appearance of the expiratory flow loop as initial expiratory flow rates rapidly decrease in the setting of obstruction. Asthma can also be diagnosed based on reversibility of bronchospasm – using β-adrenergic agonists or methacholine, PFTs will disclose alleviated (β-adrenergic agonist) or exacerbated (methacholine) obstruction. Treatment depends on the severity of asthma, with cases of intermittent asthma requiring bronchodilators as needed and elimination of triggers. Persistent asthma is treated with corticosteroids and long-acting bronchodilators, the route and choice of which depends on the severity.
incorrectExplanation: Incorrect Answers: A, C, D, E, and F. Ankylosing spondylitis (Choice A) presents with progressive skeletal rigidity of the spine which limits chest excursion during breathing, resulting in a pattern of restrictive lung disease on PFTs, marked by decreases in total lung capacity (TLC), FVC, and functional residual capacity (FRC), and residual volume (RV), with preservation of the FEV1:FVC ratio. Chronic bronchitis (Choice C) and emphysema (Choice D) are both forms of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) that are associated with a history of smoking. Chronic bronchitis is characterized by a productive cough for at least 3 months in 2 consecutive years, and emphysema is characterized by destruction of alveolar walls and enlargement of air spaces. Both conditions show an obstructive pattern on PFTs, but the history and clinical presentation differ from asthma. Extrathoracic airway obstruction (Choice E) would present with a flattening of the inspiratory loop on the flow-volume loop, and idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (Choice F) would present with a restrictive pattern on PFTs.

questionStem: A 70-year-old man comes to the office because of a 6-month history of progressive shortness of breath with exertion. Six months ago, he was able to walk five blocks before having shortness of breath. He now has shortness of breath after walking one block. He has not had chest pain, palpitations, swelling of his legs, or shortness of breath at night. He has hypertension. His medications are lisinopril and aspirin. He does not smoke cigarettes. He is a retired foundry worker. He is 183 cm (6 ft) tall and weighs 82 kg (180 lb); BMI is 24 kg/m². His pulse is 88/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 130/85 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 94%. Diffuse crackles are heard bilaterally. Cardiac examination shows no other abnormalities. There is no edema of the extremities. Results of pulmonary function testing show an FVC of 65% of predicted and an FEV₁:FVC ratio of 70%. A chest x-ray is shown. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: The patient's symptoms and pulmonary function test results are consistent with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, which is characterized by progressive shortness of breath and a restrictive pattern on pulmonary function tests.
incorrectExplanation: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease typically presents with an obstructive pattern on pulmonary function tests. Pulmonary embolism would present more acutely. Sarcoidosis and tuberculosis have different clinical and radiographic features.

questionStem: A 70-year-old man comes to the office because of a 6-month history of progressive shortness of breath with exertion. Six months ago, he was able to walk five blocks before having shortness of breath. He now has shortness of breath after walking one block. He has not had chest pain, palpitations, swelling of his legs, or shortness of breath at night. He has hypertension. His medications are lisinopril and aspirin. He does not smoke cigarettes. He is a retired foundry worker. He is 183 cm (6 ft) tall and weighs 82 kg (180 lb); BMI is 24 kg/m². His pulse is 88/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 130/85 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 94%. Diffuse crackles are heard bilaterally. Cardiac examination shows no other abnormalities. There is no edema of the extremities. Results of pulmonary function testing show an FVC of 65% of predicted and an FEV₁:FVC ratio of 70%. A chest x-ray is shown. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Pneumoconiosis describes interstitial lung disease arising because of inhalation of small solid particulate matter such as dust or powder (eg, talc, silica, beryllium, and ores) that leads to the development of fibrosis with resultant restrictive lung disease. It is often seen in patients with chronic exposures, such as foundry workers, miners, shipyard workers, cotton workers, farmers, stone drillers, and sandblasters. The disease's progress is often worsened by smoking. It generally presents with chronic symptoms of cough and shortness of breath on exertion; when severe or advanced, it can be associated with the need for supplemental oxygen and symptoms of heart failure (eg, cor pulmonale). Diagnosis is based on clinical history, symptoms, examination, exposure history, characteristic imaging tests that show fibrosis (x-ray may show honeycombing and fibrosis, especially in the apices), and pulmonary function tests that disclose a restrictive pattern of lung disease marked by decreased overall volumes and capacities but a preserved or increased ratio of FEV₁:FVC. This ratio is a key distinguishing feature from obstructive lung disease, which generally presents with a decrease in the ratio.
incorrectExplanation: Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, D, and E.

questionStem: A 55-year-old man comes to the office due to progressive shortness of breath. He has a 30-pack-year smoking history and worked as a sandblaster for 20 years. Physical examination reveals bilateral crackles. Pulmonary function tests show a decreased FEV1, decreased FEV1/FVC ratio, and decreased FVC. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Pneumoconiosis describes interstitial lung disease arising because of inhalation of small solid particulate matter such as dust or powder (eg, talc, silica, beryllium, and ores) that leads to the development of fibrosis with resultant restrictive lung disease. It is often seen in patients with chronic exposures, such as foundry workers, miners, shipyard workers, cotton workers, farmers, stone drillers, and sandblasters. The disease's progress is often worsened by smoking. This ratio is a key distinguishing feature from obstructive lung disease, which generally presents with a decrease in the ratio.
incorrectExplanation: Asbestosis (Choice A) arises because of chronic exposure to inhaled asbestos, which may cause restrictive lung disease and pneumoconiosis, with similar pulmonary function tests showing a restrictive pattern. However, on imaging, asbestosis often causes fibrosis of dependent and inferior portions of lung and is also associated with pleural thickening and nodularity. Aspergillosis (Choice B) can result in many different clinical presentations such as aspergillomas, allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis, chronic necrotizing aspergillosis, and airway invasive or angioinvasive aspergillosis. The most common are aspergillomas, which are fungal masses that arise within existing cavitary lesions of the lung, such as those caused by previous infection with tuberculosis, emphysematous blebs or bullae, or from cavitary squamous cell lung carcinoma. Asthma (Choice C), bronchiectasis (Choice D), and chronic bronchitis (Choice E) all present with an obstructive pattern on pulmonary function testing. An obstructive pattern is characterized by a decrease in FEV1, decreased FEV1:FVC ratio, and preservation of FVC. In general, these conditions also present with wheezing and air trapping on examination, as opposed to crackles.

questionStem: A 68-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department because of progressively severe cough, fever, and lethargy over the past 5 days. She has a 30-year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus and a 20-year history of rheumatoid arthritis. Her temperature is 38.4°C (101.1°F), pulse is 120/min, respirations are 28/min, and blood pressure is 128/78 mm Hg. She is lethargic. Crackles are heard at the left lung base, and there is dullness to percussion. An x-ray of the chest shows a left lower lobe infiltrate with an adjacent effusion. Pleural fluid analysis shows: Leukocyte count 50,000/mm³, Segmented neutrophils 90%, Lymphocytes 10%, Glucose 50 mg/dL, pH 6.99, Lactate dehydrogenase 212 U/L. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of these findings?
correctExplanation: Pleural effusions occur because of multiple underlying conditions including infection such as empyema, pneumonia, malignancy such as lung cancer or mesothelioma, and increased hydrostatic pressure such as left-sided heart failure. They are clinically suspected when examination discloses dullness to percussion and diminished breath sounds, and they can be visualized on imaging including chest x-ray, computerized tomography, or ultrasonography. Clinical features such as immunocompromise, history of malignancy, or infectious symptoms or signs of sepsis such as fever, tachycardia, tachypnea, and lethargy can suggest the cause. Analyzing the pleural fluid can further inform the diagnosis. Pleural fluid is analyzed for cell count, organisms, pH, glucose, total protein, and enzyme concentrations. Decreased pH and decreased glucose concentration are indicative of increased cellular metabolism in the fluid and may indicate underlying malignancy and/or infection. Fluid can be further categorized as transudate (serous fluid resulting from imbalanced hydrostatic or oncotic pressure) or exudate (complex fluid resulting from pneumonia, empyema, malignancy, or inflammatory disease) using Light's criteria, which compares the pleural fluid protein and lactate dehydrogenase concentrations to those found in serum. Empyema is characterized by an exudative effusion with increased pleural fluid leukocyte count, predominantly neutrophils, decreased glucose concentration, and decreased pH.

questionStem: A previously healthy 37-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 4-month history of abdominal cramps and diarrhea. During this period, she has had a 9-kg (20-lb) weight loss and 8 to 10 loose stools daily that contain a small amount of mucus. Abdominal examination shows mild tenderness of the right lower quadrant. A Sudan black B fat stain of the stool is positive. Colonoscopy with biopsy of the terminal ileum shows inflammation with granuloma formation. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of this patient's steatorrhea?

choices.E: Poor mixing of bile salts with dietary lipids

correctExplanation: Crohn disease is characterized by transmural inflammation of the gastrointestinal tract, most frequently involving the terminal ileum. It can arise anywhere in the gastrointestinal tract and is a subclass of inflammatory bowel disease. Most patients experience chronic abdominal cramping, bloody diarrhea, and weight loss. Examination often shows generalized abdominal tenderness, sometimes worse in the right lower quadrant, and extraintestinal manifestations such as uveitis. Severe Crohn disease can result in intestinal obstruction from stricture or inflammation, bowel perforation, intraabdominal abscess, and the formation of fistulas. Crohn disease may manifest with steatorrhea caused by the impairment of bile salt resorption secondary to inflammation of the terminal ileum. Bile salts play a crucial role in the solubilization of fats in the enteric lumen, and are recycled through the enterohepatic circulation, which is dependent on the resorption of bile salts through an intact ileal mucosa. Impairment of bile salt resorption because of ileal inflammation can overwhelm the ability of the liver to synthesize de novo bile acids, resulting in a deficiency in fat-soluble vitamin absorption. Patients with Crohn disease should undergo frequent evaluation for deficiency of fat-soluble vitamins.
incorrectExplanation: Bacterial overgrowth (Choice A) of the small bowel may occur in the setting of prior abdominal surgeries or prolonged proton-pump inhibitor use. This patient's presentation is more suggestive of fat malabsorption related to Crohn disease. Coexisting pancreatic exocrine dysfunction (Choice B) may rarely occur in association with inflammatory bowel disease, caused either by direct pancreatic inflammation or by inflammation of the intestinal wall near the pancreatic duct. However, this complication occurs less frequently than steatorrhea secondary to ileal inflammation and associated bile salt deficiency.

questionStem: A 45-year-old man comes to the office due to a 3-week history of pain and swelling in the right lower face. The pain is exacerbated by eating. The patient has no significant medical history and takes no medications. He does not use tobacco, alcohol, or illicit drugs. Temperature is 37.2 C (99 F). Physical examination shows a firm, tender swelling of the right submandibular area. The floor of the mouth is elevated on the right side. There is no lymphadenopathy. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Sialadenitis refers to inflammation of the salivary gland and typically presents with acute onset of pain and swelling over the affected gland. Acute sialadenitis often persists for several weeks and most commonly occurs because of obstruction of the gland caused by sialolithiasis but may also occur secondary to viral infection (eg, mumps or Epstein-Barr virus), bacterial infection (most commonly with S. aureus), or strictures following radiotherapy. The presence of constitutional symptoms may be indicative of a viral cause, while the expression of purulent discharge from the glandular orifice may indicate a bacterial infection. This patient's history of pain initially precipitated by meals is most suggestive of the presence of a salivary gland stone causing intermittent obstruction. Further evaluation with ultrasonography or CT may help establish the diagnosis. Treatment is primarily conservative with analgesics, application of heat and massage, and hydration. Patients that fail to improve with conservative management sometimes require removal of a sialolith, if present, usually by sialoendoscopy.
incorrectExplanation:
Mumps (Choice A) presents with salivary gland swelling, which is typically bilateral and accompanied by other signs and symptoms, such as fever, headache, malaise, and myalgia. Mumps typically presents in children and is rare in the United States because of widespread vaccination.

Sarcoidosis (Choice B) may present with parotid gland inflammation. This presentation forms part of the classic Heerfordt syndrome, along with anterior uveitis, facial nerve palsy, and fever. This manifestation of sarcoidosis is uncommon, and this patient lacks the other typical signs of Heerfordt syndrome.

Sjögren syndrome (Choice D) is an autoimmune disorder characterized by chronic inflammation and destruction of the lacrimal and salivary glands. Salivary involvement may present with chronic, painless, bilateral salivary gland enlargement.

Temporomandibular joint dysfunction (Choice E) may produce symptoms of periauricular pain and popping sensations with chewing. It does not cause facial swelling.

questionStem: An obese 42-year-old woman has an episode of colicky pain in the right upper quadrant of the abdomen that lasts 2 hours and subsides spontaneously. She has no fever or leukocytosis and no signs of peritoneal irritation in the right upper quadrant. Liver function tests show no abnormalities. Ultrasonography shows gallstones. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the abdominal pain?

choices.A: Bacterial growth in bile within the common hepatic duct
choices.B: Bacterial invasion of the gallbladder wall
choices.C: Transitory chemical irritation of the gallbladder wall
choices.D: Transitory obstruction of the common hepatic duct by gallstones
choices.E: Transitory obstruction of the cystic duct by gallstones

correctExplanation: This patient's presenting symptom of colicky pain in the right upper quadrant is consistent with biliary colic secondary to transitory obstruction of the cystic duct by gallstones. The pain is typically dull, severe, triggered by meals, and may radiate to the right shoulder. If the gallstone is passed into the common bile duct, biliary obstruction may ensue and lead to jaundice, hepatic injury, and/or acute cholangitis. Most episodes of biliary colic last for several hours before subsiding spontaneously. Biliary colic can be distinguished from cholecystitis by a lack of fever, a normal abdominal examination, and a lack of leukocytosis. Abdominal ultrasonography can aid the diagnosis by identifying the presence of gallstones. Provided that the clinical picture and examination are improving, the acute management of biliary colic is generally conservative with oral analgesics. Elective cholecystectomy is recommended to prevent future complications from the gallstones. If symptoms of biliary colic progress to show features of jaundice, hepatic injury, cholecystitis, pancreatitis, choledocholithiasis, or cholangitis, operative (cholecystectomy) or interventional (eg, endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography) management should take place.
incorrectExplanation:
Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, and D.

Bacterial growth in bile within the common hepatic duct (Choice A) may result from an ascending infection of the biliary tree, known as cholangitis, which typically occurs in the setting of biliary instrumentation or choledocholithiasis. Acute cholangitis presents with fever and jaundice in addition to abdominal pain (Charcot triad) and possibly with shock and altered mental status (Reynolds pentad).

Bacterial invasion of the gallbladder wall (Choice B) results in acute cholecystitis, which presents with fever, abdominal pain, and tenderness to palpation in the right upper quadrant, often in a patient with a history of gallstones. It is occasionally preceded by symptoms of biliary colic. Patients typically also present with leukocytosis.

questionStem: A 52-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 4-month history of loose, foul-smelling stools; during this period, he has had a 6.3-kg (14-lb) weight loss despite a good appetite. He also has had urinary frequency and urgency for 3 weeks. He has not had fever, chills, nausea, or vomiting. He has a 10-year history of recurrent alcoholic pancreatitis that required hospitalization once or twice each year because of severe abdominal pain. He has not been hospitalized since he abstained from drinking alcohol 2 years ago, but he has had chronic mild midepigastric pain since that time. During his last hospitalization 2 years ago, an x-ray of the abdomen showed calcifications in the pancreas. He is 175 cm (5 ft 9 in) tall and weighs 69 kg (153 lb); BMI is 23 kg/m2. Examination shows temporal wasting abnormalities. Abdominal examination shows midepigastric tenderness with no masses or hepatosplenomegaly; bowel sounds are normal. There is no peripheral edema. Laboratory studies show: Hematocrit 39%, Mean corpuscular volume 84 μm3, Leukocyte count 9000/mm3, Segmented neutrophils 72%, Lymphocytes 18%, Monocytes 10%, Platelet count 230,000/mm3, Serum Urea nitrogen 17 mg/dL, Glucose 280 mg/dL, Creatinine 1.2 mg/dL, Protein, total 5.8 g/dL, Albumin 2.7 g/dL. Which of the following sets of findings is the most likely explanation for this patient's increased serum glucose concentration?

choices.A: Decreased insulin production, decreased glucagon production, normal peripheral insulin response
choices.B: Decreased insulin production, increased glucagon production, normal peripheral insulin response
choices.C: Increased insulin production, decreased glucagon production, decreased peripheral insulin response
choices.D: Increased insulin production, increased glucagon production, decreased peripheral insulin response

correctExplanation: The patient's history of chronic pancreatitis and pancreatic calcifications suggests pancreatic exocrine insufficiency and endocrine dysfunction, leading to decreased insulin production. The normal peripheral insulin response indicates that insulin resistance is not the primary issue.
incorrectExplanation: Other options suggest either increased insulin production or insulin resistance, which are not consistent with the clinical picture of pancreatic insufficiency.

questionStem: Which of the following sets of findings is the most likely explanation for this patient's increased serum glucose concentration?
correctExplanation: Recurrent episodes of acute pancreatitis may lead to chronic pancreatitis and insufficiency of both the exocrine and endocrine pancreatic functions. The exocrine pancreas produces digestive enzymes, the absence of which leads to malnutrition (eg, cachexia, muscle wasting), weight loss, vitamin deficiencies, and frequent, loose, foul-smelling, sometimes oily stools (steatorrhea). The endocrine pancreas produces insulin, glucagon, and somatostatin. The loss of endogenous insulin leads to the development of diabetes mellitus with symptoms including polyuria, polydipsia, and polyphagia. In this scenario, pancreatic production of insulin and glucagon are decreased, while peripheral insulin response is normal. The diagnosis of chronic pancreatitis and pancreatic insufficiency is through clinical history, imaging, and biopsy. Exocrine pancreatic insufficiency is treated with oral pancreatic enzyme and fat-soluble vitamin replacement. Additionally, the development of diabetes mellitus caused by the loss of pancreatic insulin requires insulin replacement. Any modifiable inciting causes of pancreatitis (eg, gallstones, alcohol abuse, hypertriglyceridemia, or hypercalcemia) should be mitigated to delay disease progression and preserve remaining native pancreatic function.
incorrectExplanation: Incorrect Answers: B, C, D, E, and F.

questionStem: A 23-year-old woman comes to the office because of a 6-week history of fatigue and swelling of her eyelids, ankles, and feet. She has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. She is 163 cm (5 ft 4 in) tall and weighs 54 kg (120 lb); BMI is 21 kg/m2. Vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows 2+ periorbital edema and 3+ pedal edema. No other abnormalities are noted. Fasting serum studies show a total cholesterol concentration of 348 mg/dL and triglyceride concentration of greater than 400 mg/dL. This patient is at greatest risk for which of the following complications?
correctExplanation: Nephrotic syndrome is characterized by edema secondary to excessive proteinuria resulting in hypoalbuminemia and diminished intravascular oncotic pressure. This occurs because of the loss of normal size and charge filtration of the glomerular capillary and Bowman capsule interface. Causes of nephrotic syndrome include minimal change disease, membranous nephropathy, and focal segmental glomerulosclerosis. Minimal change disease is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children and can be idiopathic or triggered by a recent infection or immune stimulus. Patients classically present with dependent edema in the buttocks, lower back, and legs, foamy or dark-colored urine, hypoalbuminemia, hyperlipidemia, and proteinuria. Complications include hypercoagulability caused by the urinary loss of proteins such as antithrombin-3, which functions to inhibit coagulation factors II, VII, IX, X, XI, and XII. Deficiency of antithrombin-3 leads to hypercoagulability and would put this patient at high risk for thrombotic conditions such as deep venous thrombosis. Patients with nephrotic syndrome are also at an increased risk for infection because of the urinary loss of gamma globulins.
incorrectExplanation: Incorrect Answers: B, C, D, and E. Hypothyroidism (Choice B) can present with peripheral edema, but often presents with a constellation of symptoms including fatigue, cold intolerance, weight gain, hyporeflexia, and dry, cool skin. Nephrolithiasis (Choice C) can occur in settings of increased formation of calcium oxalate, uric acid, cystine, or struvite crystals. Cystine crystals occur in patients with a hereditary defect of the renal proximal convoluted tubule that results in the decreased reabsorption of cystine, ornithine, lysine, and arginine. Uric acid calculi form most commonly in patients with hyperuricemia (eg, gout) and struvite calculi occur in the setting of infections caused by urease positive microbial pathogens, such as Klebsiella or Proteus species.

questionStem: A 6-year-old boy is brought to the office due to swelling. Over the past 2 weeks, he has developed progressive swelling of his legs and abdomen. He has no significant medical history and takes no medications. His temperature is 37.2 C (99 F), blood pressure is 95/60 mm Hg, and pulse is 100/min. Physical examination shows periorbital edema and 2+ pitting edema of the bilateral lower extremities. The abdomen is distended with shifting dullness. Urinalysis shows 4+ proteinuria, but no hematuria. Serum studies show hypoalbuminemia and hyperlipidemia. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's edema?

questionStem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

correctExplanation: Acute kidney injury, a rapid decrease in renal function, may be caused by prerenal, intrinsic, or postrenal causes. Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory medications (NSAIDs) such as ibuprofen are inhibitors of cyclooxygenase (COX) enzymes, which have a primary role in the synthesis of prostaglandins and prostacyclins. These molecules play key roles in the modulation of pain sensation and thermoregulation, the maintenance of the gastric mucosal barrier, and the regulation of renal blood flow (RBF). If NSAID use occurs at higher doses, with more potent agents or over a prolonged time, acute kidney injury (AKI) can occur because of deficiency in prostaglandins, which would otherwise promote renal afferent arteriole vasodilation and RBF. AKI sustained in this manner is especially likely if high-risk NSAID use is accompanied by RBF-limiting pre-renal insults such as volume depletion. NSAIDs can also cause intrinsic acute renal injury through the risk for acute interstitial nephritis (AIN). AIN is characterized by declining urine output and glomerular filtration rate, rising creatinine, eosinophilic infiltrates on renal biopsy, and eosinophiluria. It is often associated with a rash, and is often triggered by medications including NSAIDs, diuretics, and antibiotics. In this case, this patient's rise in creatinine indicating AKI is likely caused by ibuprofen use, which should be discontinued.
incorrectExplanation: Continue ibuprofen at the current dose and repeat the laboratory studies in 2 weeks (Choice A) and continue ibuprofen at the current dose and begin oral hydrocortisone (Choice B) would be inappropriate because ibuprofen use is likely to be the cause of this patient's AKI. Switch from ibuprofen to celecoxib (Choice E) would not be appropriate because celecoxib is also an NSAID and would perpetuate, if not worsen, this patient's AKI.

questionStem: An 82-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 1-month history of urinary frequency and dribbling of small amounts of urine. He has not had pain on urination or fever. He is alert and oriented. His temperature is 36.7°C (98°F), pulse is 86/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 145/90 mm Hg. Rectal examination shows an enlarged, smooth, nontender prostate. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Bladder catheterization shows a postvoid residual volume of 750 mL. Urinalysis is within normal limits. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's incontinence?
correctExplanation: Urinary retention, nighttime overflow incontinence, an enlarged prostate, and a weak urinary stream are characteristic of benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) in older men, which can lead to bladder outlet (neck) obstruction. The best next step to relieve a bladder outlet obstruction involves catheterization to decompress the urinary bladder and prevent acute complications of prolonged bladder outlet obstruction such as bladder rupture, urothelial cell atrophy or necrosis, hydroureter, hydronephrosis, post-renal azotemia, and/or renal failure. A post-void residual volume of urine should generally be less than 50–100 mL, and significant urinary retention beyond 200–250 mL (though clinical guidelines vary) is generally an indication for placement of a urinary catheter to relieve obstruction.
incorrectExplanation: Detrusor muscle hyperactivity (Choice B) defines overactive bladder and uninhibited bladder contractions. It commonly results in urge incontinence, which presents with the urge to void followed by the leakage of urine. It does not necessarily occur with a large volume of urine in the bladder. Neurogenic bladder (Choice C) is often caused by spinal cord injuries or primary nervous system pathology (eg, multiple sclerosis) with loss of appropriate interplay between the signals from the sympathetic, parasympathetic, and somatic nervous system, all of which are required for appropriately coordinated bladder filling and emptying. In this patient, overflow incontinence caused by bladder outlet obstruction from benign prostatic hyperplasia is more likely. Neurogenic bladder often presents as urge or overflow incontinence, depending on the aspect of neural control which is dysregulated. A prostatic infection (Choice D) can present with incontinence as well as dysuria and a tender, boggy prostate on examination. A urinalysis would be abnormal and show numerous leukocytes and bacteria. Urethral hypermobility (Choice E) is a common cause of stress incontinence in women. It occurs when the pelvic floor muscles and ligaments that support the urethra and bladder neck weaken, leading to involuntary leakage of urine during activities that increase intra-abdominal pressure (eg, coughing, sneezing, laughing).

questionStem: A 67-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 2-day history of fever, nausea, a continuous urge to void, and progressive difficulty with urination. Every 30 minutes, he passes a small amount of urine and has an uncomfortable burning sensation. He says he has slept poorly during this period. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial step in management?
correctExplanation: Placement of a urinary catheter is the most appropriate initial step in management for this patient who is likely experiencing acute urinary retention due to benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH). questionStem: A 72-year-old man comes to the emergency department due to 2 days of fever, dysuria, and urinary frequency. He has had difficulty urinating for the past several months, with a weak urinary stream and dribbling at the end of urination. He has also had several episodes of nocturia and urinary incontinence. The patient has a history of hypertension and hyperlipidemia. His temperature is 38.3 C (100.9 F), blood pressure is 150/90 mm Hg, and pulse is 92/min. Physical examination shows suprapubic fullness and a distended bladder. Laboratory results reveal a serum creatinine level of 2.1 mg/dL. Urinalysis shows numerous white blood cells and bacteria. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
correctExplanation: This patient's urinary retention, nighttime overflow incontinence, an enlarged prostate, and a weak urinary stream is suggestive of bladder outlet obstruction from benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH). As shown in this patient, BPH can result in complications such as urinary tract infection, as evidenced by fever, dysuria, and white blood cells on urinalysis. In addition, severe bladder outlet obstruction can result in a postrenal acute kidney injury and increased serum creatinine level. The first appropriate step in management is relief of the bladder outlet obstruction by placement of a urinary catheter. The already narrowed prostatic urethra, if affected by secondary inflammation or infection, can result in near complete bladder outflow obstruction. Impaired drainage of the bladder and urethra predisposes to infection by limiting urinary washout of ascending pathogens, often enteric organisms.
incorrectExplanation: Ultrasonography of the kidneys (Choice A) would be helpful in evaluating for severity and laterality of hydronephrosis in the setting of a urinary tract obstruction but would not be an appropriate first step, which should be focused on urgent treatment of the outlet obstruction. Similarly, CT scan of the pelvis (Choice B) can help with identifying and characterizing anatomical causes of outlet obstruction, but further diagnostic strategies should not take priority over alleviating obstruction. Furosemide therapy (Choice C) is used in the treatment of hypervolemia, which would not be appropriate in this patient who has no signs of lower extremity edema, pulmonary edema, ascites, or other signs of volume overload. Furosemide, a diuretic, may also increase the severity of acute kidney injury in this patient by reducing volume status and decreasing renal blood flow. Levofloxacin therapy (Choice D) would be appropriate in the management of this patient's urinary tract infection secondary to outlet obstruction. First, the outlet obstruction must be addressed. Hemodialysis (Choice F) would be appropriate in patients with severe acute kidney injury resulting in volume overload, severe electrolyte abnormalities such as hyperkalemia, uremia, or acidosis. While this patient may require dialysis, addressing the urinary outlet obstruction first may rapidly improve renal function.

questionStem: Which of the following is the most appropriate antibiotic for treating a patient with Neisseria gonorrhoeae infection?
correctExplanation: Neisseria gonorrhoeae can cause vaginitis, cervicitis, and pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) in women. It can also cause a multifocal dermatitis that typically presents with tender macular and/or pustular lesions along with disseminated and migratory polyarthritis. Risk factors for PID and other sexually transmitted infections include adolescence, multiple sexual partners, and not using barrier contraception such as condoms. Vaginitis typically presents with mucopurulent discharge and pruritus. Cervicitis presents with similar discharge but also with an erythematous, friable cervix and cervical motion tenderness on examination. When infection spreads to the fallopian tubes and ovaries, PID with purulent cervical discharge, uterine and adnexal tenderness, and systemic symptoms such as fever can result. If left untreated, PID can be complicated by tubo-ovarian or intraabdominal abscess, presenting with focal tenderness and a fluctuant mass. The antibiotic treatment of Neisseria gonorrhoeae infection involves the use of third generation cephalosporins such as ceftriaxone, as well as concurrent treatment of Chlamydia trachomatis with doxycycline.
incorrectExplanation: Azithromycin (Choice A) would treat an infection from Chlamydia trachomatis or trichomoniasis, as well as bacterial vaginosis. However, it does not provide appropriate antimicrobial coverage for Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Nafcillin (Choice C) is used to treat gram-positive organisms, especially methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus. It is not the antibiotic of choice to treat Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Penicillin (Choice D) is the treatment of choice for syphilis, which is a sexually transmitted disease from the spirochete Treponema pallidum that can present in multiple stages. Primarily syphilis presents with a painless chancre (ulcer) of the genitalia. Secondary syphilis can present with macular, not pustular lesions of the hands and feet. Syphilis would not typically cause vaginal discharge. Vancomycin (Choice E) would not appropriately cover the causative organisms of vaginitis. It is effective in the treatment of resistant organisms such as methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus and ampicillin-resistant Enterococcus spp. It does not have significant activity against Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Educational Objective: Neisseria gonorrhoeae can cause vaginitis, cervicitis, PID, and a multifocal dermatitis that typically presents with tender macular and/or pustular lesions. Ceftriaxone is the antibiotic of choice for Neisseria gonorrhoeae.

questionStem: A 28-year-old woman comes to the office because of an 8-week history of fatigue and cold intolerance. She has a 2-year history of bipolar disorder. At the age of 4 years, she was hospitalized for 2 days for treatment of meningitis. At the age of 16 years, she had loss of consciousness after a motor vehicle collision. Her medications are divalproex, an oral contraceptive, and a daily multivitamin. Her brother has type 1 diabetes mellitus. The patient does not smoke cigarettes. She drinks two 12-oz beers daily and smokes marijuana four times monthly. She appears well developed and well nourished. Her temperature is 36.4°C (97.5°F), pulse is 54/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 120/74 mm Hg. The thyroid gland is nontender and cannot be palpated. Deep tendon reflexes are 2+. The remainder of the examination, including cardiac examination, shows no abnormalities. Serum studies show a thyroid-stimulating hormone concentration of 23 μU/mL and free thyroxine concentration of 0.5 ng/dL (N=0.8–2.4). Which of the following historical factors has most likely increased this patient's risk for her current condition?
correctExplanation: This patient's family history of a brother with type 1 diabetes mellitus is the most important historical clue because it suggests an increased risk for familial autoimmune disease. While there are many varieties of thyroid disease that can lead to hypothyroidism, the most common cause of hypothyroidism in iodine-replete parts of the world is Hashimoto thyroiditis, also known as chronic autoimmune thyroiditis. Lymphocytic infiltration of the thyroid gland leads to cytotoxic destruction of the gland and subsequent fibrosis, which results in hypothyroidism. Patients may either have a goiter or a normal size thyroid gland. The diagnosis is made by measuring the thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) concentration, which will be increased, and the free thyroxine concentration (FT4), which will be decreased. This pattern indicates adequate secretion of TSH from the pituitary gland but inadequate production of thyroxine in the thyroid gland. In some cases, patients may have antibodies against thyroid peroxidase or thyroglobulin, although these are not required for diagnosis. As this is an autoimmune disease, patients with a family history of other autoimmune disorders such as type 1 diabetes mellitus and primary adrenal insufficiency are at greater risk for developing chronic autoimmune thyroiditis. Treatment is with thyroid hormone replacement in the form of levothyroxine.
incorrectExplanation: Alcohol consumption (Choice A) does not increase the risk for developing hypothyroidism.

questionStem: A 42-year-old woman is admitted to the hospital because of a 1-month history of burning and tingling of the skin over all the extremities and fatigue. She has hypertension and chronic low back pain. Her only medication is hydrochlorothiazide. She appears tired but is not in acute distress. Her temperature is 37.2°C (99°F), pulse is 88/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 110/80 mm Hg. Tapping over the facial nerve produces an involuntary contraction of the ipsilateral muscles. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Serum studies show: Na+ 138 mEq/L, K+ 4.1 mEq/L, Cl- 100 mEq/L, Ca2+ 7.1 mg/dL, Phosphate 6 mg/dL, Protein, total 9 g/dL, Albumin 5 g/dL. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this patient's condition?
correctExplanation: Deficiency of parathyroid hormone (PTH), also known as hypoparathyroidism, likely explains this patient's symptomatic hypocalcemia. PTH is a peptide hormone that increases osteoclast activity and bone resorption to maintain calcium homeostasis. It is produced by the four parathyroid glands, which are located on the posterior aspect of the thyroid gland. Primary hypoparathyroidism can occur following the unintentional resection of the parathyroid glands during thyroidectomy or may be caused by autoimmune destruction of the parathyroid glands. Primary hypoparathyroidism results in decreased concentrations of PTH, which leads to hypocalcemia secondary to inadequate bone resorption, hyperphosphatemia, and decreased concentrations of 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (calcitriol) because PTH stimulates renal conversion of 25-hydroxyvitamin D to its active form. Decreased concentrations of calcitriol substantially worsen hypocalcemia as calcitriol directly stimulates intestinal calcium absorption. Signs and symptoms of severe hypocalcemia include perioral tingling, muscle cramps, and carpopedal spasm.

questionStem: A 45-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 2-week history of muscle cramps and tingling in her hands and feet. She underwent a total thyroidectomy 3 weeks ago for treatment of papillary thyroid carcinoma. Her blood pressure is 120/80 mm Hg, pulse is 80/min, and respirations are 16/min. Physical examination shows a positive Chvostek sign. Laboratory studies show a serum calcium concentration of 7.0 mg/dL and a serum phosphorus concentration of 5.5 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's laboratory findings?
correctExplanation: Deficiency of parathyroid hormone (PTH), also known as hypoparathyroidism, likely explains this patient's symptomatic hypocalcemia. Decreased concentrations of calcitriol substantially worsen hypocalcemia as calcitriol directly stimulates intestinal calcium absorption. Signs and symptoms of severe hypocalcemia may include perioral paresthesia, carpopedal spasm, laryngospasm, and prolonged QT interval. The Chvostek sign, in which tapping of the facial nerve leads to spasm of the facial muscles, and Trousseau sign, in which an inflated blood pressure cuff occluding the brachial artery causes carpopedal spasm, are two physical examination signs that may indicate hypocalcemia. Treatment of primary hypoparathyroidism is with calcium and calcitriol supplementation to achieve a low-normal calcium level.
incorrectExplanation:
Incorrect Answers: A, B, D, E, and F.

Autonomous secretion of aldosterone (Choice A), known as primary hyperaldosteronism, usually results in hypokalemia, alkalosis, and hypertension. This patient's serum potassium is normal, and her blood pressure is also within a normal range.

Autonomous secretion of parathyroid hormone (Choice B) is known as primary hyperparathyroidism and results in hypercalcemia, not hypocalcemia. Symptoms of hypercalcemia may include weakness, constipation, confusion, depression, diffuse bone pain, nephrolithiasis, and polyuria.

Deficiency of vitamin B12 (cobalamin) (Choice D) can lead to paresthesia and reduced proprioception because of subacute combined degeneration of the dorsal and lateral columns of the spinal cord. Patients present with impaired gait, an abnormal Romberg test, and macrocytic anemia with macrocytic anemia.

Vitamin D excess can lead to hypercalcemia, not hypocalcemia.

Her menses were normal until 1 year ago when they became irregular. She has not had a menstrual period for the past 6 months. She has also had a small amount of milky secretion from her breasts. She does not take medications. Her vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows no abnormalities except for galactorrhea. Her serum prolactin concentration is 200 ng/mL. A pregnancy test is negative. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?

correctExplanation: MRI of the pituitary gland is the most appropriate next step in evaluation of this young woman with amenorrhea, galactorrhea, and an increased serum concentration of prolactin. This medication is routinely used for women who desire pregnancy, as in this case, although bromocriptine is a reasonable alternative. questionStem: A 32-year-old woman comes to the emergency department 12 hours after the sudden onset of fever, diffuse muscle and bone pain, and dizziness. questionStem: An 82-year-old woman comes to the office because of a 3-week history of bilateral frontal headaches and a 3-day history of pain over the parietal skull regions. She also has claudication of the jaw and tongue after she chews vigorously. Examination and complete blood count 6 months ago showed no abnormalities. Today, her temperature is 38.5°C (101.3°F), pulse is 90/min and regular, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 160/85 mm Hg. On physical examination, there is tenderness of the temporal regions bilaterally with the left more tender than the right. Results of laboratory studies show: Hematocrit 27% Mean corpuscular volume 87 μm³ Leukocyte count 5800/mm³ with a normal differential Platelet count 450,000/mm³ Erythrocyte sedimentation rate 78 mm/h Which of the following is the most likely ophthalmic complication of this disorder?
correctExplanation: Granulomatous arteritis in cervical or temporal arteries, also referred to as temporal or giant cell arteritis is a vasculitis that affects the large vessels such as the aorta, aortic arch vessels, the temporal branch of the external carotid, and vertebral arteries, among others. It is characterized by headache, temporal tenderness, jaw claudication, and fever. A potential complication includes monocular blindness from ischemic optic neuropathy. This occurs secondary to inflammation and resultant thrombosis of the central retinal artery and/or posterior ciliary arteries. Because of this potential acute complication, this condition requires the urgent administration of glucocorticoids, ophthalmologic evaluation, and temporal artery biopsy for diagnosis. Administration of steroids does not generally affect biopsy results if biopsy occurs within 1 to 2 weeks.
incorrectExplanation: Dendritic corneal ulceration (Choice A) can be seen in herpes simplex virus keratitis, which can cause conjunctivitis and blepharoconjunctivitis. It is not related to temporal arteritis.

questionStem: A 27-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 6-month history of her hands and fingers becoming tender and turning white on exposure to cold. The symptoms occur four times monthly. She has not had any other symptoms. She has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. She has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 8 years. Examination shows no abnormalities. Results of laboratory studies are within the reference range. In addition to smoking cessation, which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation?
correctExplanation: Vasospasm causes the intermittent loss of blood flow to the distal extremities in Raynaud phenomenon, resulting in sequential white, blue, and red discoloration of the affected areas of skin. The vasospasm associated with Raynaud phenomenon can be triggered and exacerbated by cold temperature, stress, or emotional upset. Activities such as cigarette smoking, injury, trauma, or chemical exposure can put patients at a higher risk for Raynaud phenomenon. Raynaud phenomenon may be idiopathic or associated with mixed connected tissue disease, systemic lupus erythematosus, or CREST syndrome. When severe or prolonged, ischemic injury can result in digital ulcerations. Dressing warmly in cold weather can help prevent Raynaud phenomenon by decreasing cold exposure.

Incorrect Answers: B, C, D, and E.

Doxazosin (Choice B) is an α-adrenergic blocker that can help treat hypertension, post-traumatic stress disorder, and urinary retention from benign prostatic hyperplasia. It has not been conclusively shown to improve symptoms of Raynaud phenomenon.

Prednisone therapy (Choice C) is a glucocorticoid used in a variety of systemic inflammatory conditions such as scleroderma, which can be associated with Raynaud phenomenon, but it would not directly address the mechanism of vasospasm.

Propranolol therapy (Choice D) is a non-selective β-adrenergic blocker that is used in the treatment of hypertension, hyperthyroidism, anxiety disorders, and portal hypertension. It is not generally employed in the treatment of Raynaud phenomenon.

questionStem: A 27-year-old man, who works for a lawn maintenance service, is brought to the emergency department by his supervisor 10 minutes after he was found incoherent and wandering around the neighborhood where they were working in the late afternoon. His supervisor reports that the patient was fine when he arrived at work at 6:30 AM, but no one could locate him after they took a lunch break at noon. The temperature outside is 103°F. He takes an over-the-counter antihistamine for severe allergies. His father died of a myocardial infarction at the age of 39 years. His mother and sister have autoimmune thyroiditis. He is alert but not oriented to person, place, or time. His temperature is 39.4°C (103°F), pulse is 100/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 120/68 mm Hg. Examination shows warm, dry skin. The pupils are 4 mm and sluggishly reactive. Neurologic examination shows no muscle rigidity. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Heat stroke is characterized by an increased body temperature that occurs when the body is exposed to high environmental temperatures and high humidity. It commonly happens in young athletes or in elderly patients with impaired thermoregulatory capacity. Excessive heat exposure and increased core body temperature lead to cardiovascular and neurologic dysfunction with secondary tachycardia, tachypnea, and hypotension. Vasodilation of superficial blood vessels may lead to shunting of blood with resultant multi-organ system dysfunction, including neurologic impairment, hepatic and renal ischemia, rhabdomyolysis, and disseminated intravascular coagulation. Treatment includes cooling of the patient with fans or ice water, continuous core temperature monitoring, and support of the patient’s airway, breathing, and circulation. A patient must demonstrate neurologic symptoms to diagnose heat stroke, whereas heat exhaustion presents similarly but with an intact neurologic examination. In this example, the patient is a young manual laborer who works outside in the sun; his use of an antihistamine (especially if it also has anticholinergic action) may also impair his ability to thermoregulate through sweat and cutaneous vasodilation.
incorrectExplanation: Incorrect Answers: B, C, D, and E. Malignant hyperthermia (Choice B) is characterized by rigidity, hyperthermia, and autonomic instability, often in the operative or post-operative setting following the administration of volatile inhaled anesthetics, such as halothane or isoflurane, or paralytics such as succinylcholine. Myocardial ischemia (Choice C) presents with chest pain, shortness of breath, and ST-segment elevation or depression or T-wave inversion on ECG. Hyperthermia and neurologic symptoms are not typical. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (Choice D) is characterized by hyperthermia, autonomic dysregulation, altered mental status, and generalized muscle rigidity. It occurs in patients taking antipsychotic medications. Thyroid storm (Choice E) is characterized by hyperthermia, tachycardia, hypertension, and altered mental status in a patient with hyperthyroidism. This patient has no history of hyperthyroidism.

questionStem: A 74-year-old woman is admitted to the hospital following a myocardial infarction. She is confused and has cool, clammy skin. Over the next hour, her blood pressure decreases from 148/74 mm Hg to 80/40 mm Hg. Arterial blood gas analysis is most likely to show which of the following?
correctExplanation: Following a myocardial infarction, hypotension, altered mental status, and hypoperfused (cool, clammy) skin is most likely caused by cardiogenic shock. Cardiogenic shock is caused by a decrease in cardiac output, often caused by infarcted or infected cardiac muscle. This leads to vasoconstriction of peripheral vessels to maintain blood pressure and inadequate perfusion of end organs. As organs begin to receive an insufficient supply of oxygen, they transition from aerobic metabolism to anaerobic metabolism, which leads to the production of lactic acid. This lactic acid decreases the pH of the blood, leading to a metabolic acidosis. This is often worsened in cardiogenic shock because the liver is unable to adequately metabolize lactate in the setting of decreased perfusion. Therefore, this patient likely has a metabolic acidosis caused by the production of lactic acid.
incorrectExplanation: Hypoxemia with normal pH (Choice A) can be seen with primarily lung pathologies, such as an asthma or COPD exacerbation. However, prolonged hypoxemia often leads to a metabolic acidosis caused by an inadequate supply of oxygen to tissues, causing transition to anaerobic metabolism with consequent lactate production. This patient is more likely to have a metabolic acidosis related to decreased cardiac output than persistent hypoxemia with a normal pH. Metabolic alkalosis (Choice C) is often associated with the loss of acid, often from the gastrointestinal tract. For example, persistent emesis can cause metabolic alkalosis, as can the use of diuretics. This patient has no clear source of a loss of hydrogen ions, making metabolic alkalosis unlikely. Respiratory acidosis (Choice D) can be acute or chronic. Acute respiratory acidosis is often caused by hypoventilation, such as in the case of opioid-induced respiratory depression. Chronic, compensated respiratory acidosis is more commonly seen in patients with obstructive lung disease or obesity hypoventilation syndrome. This patient's cardiogenic shock would not lead to a respiratory acidosis.

questionStem: A 65-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because of confusion and lethargy. He has a history of coronary artery disease and hypertension. His blood pressure is 80/60 mm Hg, pulse is 120/min, and respirations are 24/min. Physical examination shows cool, clammy skin. Laboratory studies show: Arterial blood gas: pH 7.25, PCO2 30 mm Hg, PO2 60 mm Hg, HCO3- 14 mEq/L. Which of the following is the most likely acid-base disturbance in this patient?

It can also occur in other forms of shock, such as hypovolemic or septic, also caused by the inadequate supply of oxygen to the body's tissues.

questionStem: A 52-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because of a 1-day history of fever and chills. He received the diagnosis of small cell carcinoma of the lung 1 month ago and is undergoing chemotherapy. A right subclavian central venous catheter is in place. His temperature is 38.9°C (102.1°F), pulse is 124/min, respirations are 24/min, and blood pressure is 104/68 mm Hg. Examination shows warm, flushed skin. The catheter site is slightly erythematous, and there is tenderness over the subcutaneous pocket. His leukocyte count is 12,300/mm³. A chest x-ray shows a nodule in the right upper lobe. Which of the following is the most likely causal organism?
correctExplanation: Bacteremia commonly presents with fevers, tachycardia, tachypnea, hypotension, and leukocytosis, and can also be associated with altered mental status and end organ damage if it proceeds to cause septic shock. While it can be caused by a variety of infections, such as pneumonia or pyelonephritis, it is most likely caused by this patient's central line given its erythematous and tender insertion site. Central line catheters are most often placed for the administration of vasopressors in critically ill patients, as an alternative for venous access in patients with difficult to obtain peripheral access, and for the long-term administration of medications, such as antibiotics or chemotherapy. Unfortunately, central line-associated bloodstream infections are a relatively common complication. Bacteria, most often skin flora such as staphylococcal species, can be introduced into the bloodstream and lead to bacteremia, especially in patients who are immunocompromised, such as this patient undergoing chemotherapy. Therefore, the most likely causal organism in this patient is Staphylococcus epidermidis, a common cutaneous organism that can translocate and seed discontinuities in skin such as line sites. Treatment includes intravenous antibiotics and removal of the line.
incorrectExplanation:
Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, and D.

Candida albicans (Choice A) is a fungal organism that most commonly causes oropharyngeal candidiasis, esophagitis, and vulvovaginitis. Candidemia, or the invasion of Candida into the blood, is rare and often only seen in immunocompromised patients, with other risk factors including admission to the ICU, central line access, and the administration of total parenteral nutrition. However, candidemia often leads to severe sepsis with associated skin and ophthalmologic lesions, which this patient does not have.

Clostridium perfringens (Choice B) is a common pathogen in necrotizing skin infections, which present with fever, pain out of proportion to examination, erythema, ecchymosis, edema, and bullae, often in immunocompromised or diabetic patients. It progresses rapidly over hours to days and requires emergent surgical debridement as it can lead to septic shock.

questionStem: A 37-year-old woman comes to the physician for HIV screening. She is asymptomatic. She has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. She does not drink alcohol or use illicit drugs. She has had two lifetime male sexual partners, and they used condoms consistently. Examination shows no abnormalities. An ELISA is positive for HIV; the sensitivity of the ELISA is 95%, and the specificity is 90%. Which of the following represents the most appropriate sensitivity and specificity of an additional test to confirm this patient's diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Sensitivity and specificity are important concepts when determining which diagnostic tests to utilize and how to interpret them. Sensitivity refers to the ability of a test to correctly identify those with the disease, whereas specificity refers to the ability of a test to correctly identify those without the disease. In a patient population with low prevalence of a disease, a negative result on a highly sensitive test can effectively rule out the disease because there is a low rate of false negative tests. However, a positive result on a sensitive test must be verified by a highly specific test, which would have a decreased risk for false positive results. Therefore, sensitive tests are often used for screening, as in this patient, but must be verified by a more specific test. Therefore, a test with 99% specificity would be most likely to confirm or refute this patient's diagnosis. Specificity is calculated as true negatives divided by the sum of true negatives and false positives. Therefore, a test with a 99% specificity would have only one false positive out of 100 administered tests. Positive tests would therefore be more likely to be true positives.
incorrectExplanation: While tests A, B, and C are all highly sensitive, a diagnosis is more appropriately confirmed by a test with high specificity because it can more reliably determine who does not have the disease. Therefore, a positive result on a highly specific test is more likely to be indicative of disease.

questionStem: A study is conducted to assess a possible association between regular use of alcohol and colon cancer. Cases consist of patients hospitalized with colon cancer; controls consist of age- and gender-matched patients admitted to the same hospital for treatment of an acute injury. Cases and controls are interviewed after their conditions stabilize. The researchers conclude that regular use of alcohol reduced the risk of colon cancer. Which of the following is the most important reason to be concerned about the authors' conclusion?

choices.D: Lack of incidence rates for alcohol users and nonusers

correctExplanation: A variety of methodological flaws or study weaknesses can limit the application of study results to a general population. These flaws include confounding variables, inappropriate selection of case or control groups, inappropriate analysis of data, and biases, such as sampling bias and observation bias. In designing a case control study to determine relationships between exposures and outcomes, it is important to choose a case group and a control group that are matched to eliminate or avoid confounding to strengthen conclusions that differences observed are caused by the variables being studied. For example, in this scenario, choosing a control population that consists of patients admitted to the hospital with acute injuries likely interferes with the interpreted results of the studies that the regular use of alcohol reduced the risk for colon cancer. This is because regular alcohol use can lead to acute injuries during intoxication, and thus the control group may have a higher baseline use of alcohol compared to the case group. This has likely led to the possible inappropriate conclusion in this study that regular use of alcohol reduced the risk for colon cancer. Therefore, the most important reason to be concerned about the authors' conclusion of this study is the inappropriate control group.
incorrectExplanation:
Incorrect Answers: A, B, and D.

Confounding by age (Choice A) was not present in this study because the control and case group were matched by age, which would eliminate age as a confounding variable.

Inappropriate case group (Choice B) is not correct. As the authors were interested in determining the effects of regular alcohol use on colon cancer, choosing a group of patients with colon cancer is an appropriate case group for this study. This group can then be interviewed about their use of alcohol, which can be compared to the use of alcohol in an appropriate control group to determine whether regular alcohol use is linked to the development of colon cancer.

Lack of incidence rates for alcohol users and nonusers (Choice D) is not the most concerning aspect of this study. Incidence rates would be more important in evaluating the risk for developing colon cancer, which is not the focus of this case control study. The risk of colon cancer is not being evaluated in this study.

questionStem: A 75-year-old man with terminal heart failure is brought to the emergency department due to worsening back pain. He has had multiple hospitalizations over the past year for heart failure exacerbations and has been intubated twice. The patient is now unable to walk due to pain and weakness. He is alert and oriented. His blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg, pulse is 88/min, and respirations are 16/min. Physical examination shows bilateral lower extremity weakness and decreased sensation to pinprick below the umbilicus. The patient has decided to enroll in hospice care. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
correctExplanation: Hospice care is a form of health care that aims to provide comfort and palliation to terminally ill patients in their last stages of life. As a terminally ill patient approaches the end of life, they may decide to focus on the quality of remaining life rather than on increasing the quantity of time remaining. Hospice is a multidisciplinary healthcare model that includes physicians, nurses, social workers, and chaplains and aids to eliminate suffering and provide spiritual and emotional support to patients and their family.
